title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (6 of 7)
hook: arise, awake; the path is sharp as a razor's edge
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two paths in one picture: the chariot of the self. Rider, charioteer, reins and horses. Did you feel for the reins once? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Have you ever been woken by someone who really needed you up? Not a gentle alarm. A hand on the shoulder, a voice: get up, now. There's one verse in the Katha that sounds exactly like that. Swami Vivekananda made it famous in modern India, and it still shows up on school walls, posters and the covers of notebooks. You may have seen it without knowing it came from the house of Death.
screen: `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `GET UP, NOW.` → `FROM THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Right after the chariot, Yama says: uttishthata, jagrata. Arise! Awake! Having reached the great teachers, learn. And then a warning: the path is sharp as the edge of a razor, hard to cross, hard to walk, say the wise. A razor's edge: step carelessly and you're cut. That doesn't mean it's cruel. It means it's narrow. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't done once; it's done step by step, with attention. A few verses later, Yama explains why the path is hard. The self-existent one, he says, pierced the openings of the senses outward. So we look outward, not at the self within. Our eyes, ears and attention point away from ourselves, by design. But some wise person, wishing for the deathless, turned their eyes inward and saw the self. The phrase is often translated as turning the gaze around. And he gives a picture of what's seen: a person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body, like a flame without smoke. Lord of past and future. The same today and tomorrow. So here are three ways the Katha says the same thing. Arise, awake: you've been sleepwalking toward the pleasant. The razor's edge: the good path is narrow and needs care. The inward gaze: the senses face out, and the good path turns them back. None of it is gloomy. A flame without smoke is a warm picture. It's what's waiting when you stop looking only outward.
screen: `ARISE! AWAKE!` · `SHARP AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `THE SENSES FACE OUTWARD.` · `A FLAME WITHOUT SMOKE.` · then, large: `TURN THE GAZE AROUND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Open your eyes and notice how naturally they go outward, to the room, the light, whatever moves. Now close them, and, just for a moment, turn the gaze around. Not looking at anything. Feeling the place you look from. Some people find it helps to picture a small, steady flame in the center of the chest, smokeless and warm. If that picture helps, rest with it. If not, just rest behind your closed eyes. The bell holds the time.
The two paths. The good one is sharp as a razor's edge, and it turns the gaze inward. Arise, awake, and learn.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Today, once, when you reach for something outside yourself to feel better, turn inward for one breath first. Day two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Katha 1.3.14, 'uttishthata jagrata', was popularized by Swami Vivekananda as a call to awaken, and is widely quoted in India on schools, in speeches and in youth movements.

match.prompt: three ways of saying it — tap the pairs.
pairs: the path is narrow, hard to walk

myth: 'arise, awake' was first said by Vivekananda
it's Katha 1.3.14; Vivekananda made it famous in modern India.
the Katha says the senses were made to face outward
so we look outward, not within; the wise turn the gaze around.

fork.setup: your senses all face outward. you want to see the self. what does the wise person in the Katha do?
fork.reveal: wishing for the deathless, the wise one turned the eyes inward, and saw the self.

original.note: Sanskrit: uttishthata, arise! (plural); Katha 1.3.14: uttishthata jagrata, arise, awake.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'arise, awake' is a modern motivational slogan.
what it means: it's Death's call to wake up to the self, on a path sharp as a razor's edge.
what a scholar hears: 1.3.14 continues prapya varan nibodhata, having reached the great ones, learn; 2.1.1 says the self-existent pierced the senses outward (parañci khani).

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (arise, awake; the razor's edge)
